item.title: Housing demand up 8.2% in Q2FY27 on festive cheer: Magicbricks report
item.description: Magicbricks' PropIndex report showed housing demand rose 8.2 per cent in July-September 2026, with premium homes gaining traction, though demand stayed below year-ago levels ...
item.dc:creator: Akshat Ayush
item.content:encoded: India’s residential property market witnessed an improvement in buyer sentiment with the festive season in sight as housing demand rose 8.2 per cent between July and September 2026, according to Magicbricks’ PropIndex report. Major residential markets registered an increase in demand in Q2FY27 as property prices rose marginally. However, demand remained below year-ago levels. “The latest PropIndex findings reflect strengthening demand across key residential markets, alongside growing interest in premium housing. Homebuyers continue to prioritise location, space and value, while varying supply and price trends highlight the importance of local market dynamics,” Prasun Kumar, CMO at Magicbricks, said. Homes priced above ₹3 crore recorded notable demand growth in Greater Noida, Bengaluru and Noida. Magicbricks said this pointed to continued interest in higher-value properties, while also reflecting the varied nature of buyer demand, with premium housing gaining traction alongside sustained interest in more practical home configurations. Homebuyer preferences continued to centre on mid-sized homes, the report added. Properties measuring 750–1,250 square feet (sq ft) accounted for the largest share of demand, followed by homes in the 1,250–2,000 sq ft category. Together, these segments represented more than two-thirds of overall demand. Meanwhile, two-bedroom and three-bedroom apartments remained the most preferred configurations, highlighting buyers’ focus on balancing space requirements with location and overall value. On the supply side, active property listings registered a modest increase nationally, with Bengaluru recording the strongest growth among the highlighted markets, followed by Noida and Hyderabad. In contrast, available listings contracted in Gurugram, Chennai and Ahmedabad. Magicbricks said the variation in supply trends across cities indicated that market conditions continued to differ by geography, with some markets seeing an expansion in available inventory while others remained relatively constrained. Property prices continued to rise, with Mumbai and Chennai recording some of the strongest quarterly increases, followed by Ahmedabad and Bengaluru. Prices remained relatively stable in Greater Noida and Gurugram, reflecting differing demand-supply dynamics across residential markets.

item.title: Flexibility for AIFs is not relaxation but more responsibility: Sebi WTM
item.description: Sebi whole-time member Sandip Pradhan said regulation of private markets will increasingly need to be proportionate, data-driven and risk-based as the sector expands ...
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: Regulatory flexibility for alternative investment funds (AIFs) should be seen as a transfer of greater responsibility to the industry, rather than merely a relaxation of norms, Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) whole-time member Sandip Pradhan said on Wednesday. Speaking at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) summit on alternative investments, Pradhan said regulation would increasingly need to be data-driven and risk-based. “Today, the challenge is more nuanced. On one hand, the industry is seeking greater flexibility in areas such as investment structures, co-investment, leverage, governance arrangements and differentiated rights for sophisticated investors. On the other hand, the growing size and interconnectedness of private markets require us to pay greater attention to governance, conflicts of interest, valuation transparency and investor protection. Hence, we need to strike a balance,” he said. Pradhan outlined three key priorities for the sector: proportionate regulation, improved data and risk-based supervision, and stronger governance. On governance, he said investment committees, compliance officers, trustees and senior management must ensure that regulatory flexibility is exercised responsibly. He urged the industry to come forward with “rigorous, data-backed” proposals, adding that a responsive regulatory framework could be co-created only through mature and proactive submissions. Pradhan also said a circular detailing the approved changes to the accreditation framework would be issued soon. The number of accredited investors currently stands at about 2,000, compared with roughly 100,000 AIF investors. The proposed changes could increase the number of accredited investors to about 400,000, the Sebi whole-time member added.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels

IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva | Image: Bloomberg

AP Bangkok 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:08 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday that the US and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing heaviest on low-income countries and straining the global financial system. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognise that the federal deficit and national debt have grown too high, just trying to grow the US economy out of its more than USD 40 trillion in national debt would not suffice. "At the fund, we believe that, growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

"There is no magic," she said, noting some other measures would be needed. "You have to go in a direction of tightening that, bringing it down, bringing deficit down." Fiscal consolidation' faces challenges Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world's poorest nations. Also Read

Best of Opinion: Global growth headline numbers mask vulnerabilities

Global growth resilience premium

AI investment props up global growth, but war, debt threaten outlook: IMF

IMF raises India's growth forecast to 7% in FY27 on strong domestic demand

Global economy nears limits of resilience as energy squeeze persists: IMF

Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call "fiscal consolidation" have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. "Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries," said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. "And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world."   "Among the world's poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance," the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said.

That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. Nations need help with job creation, investment "We know that today the median developing country is going to pay, is actually today paying three times more on their interest repayments than developed countries," Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme, said in an interview with The Associated Press. On average nearly 10 per cent of government spending is going to repay debt, and the combination of high prices for fuel, fertiliser and other needs, the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon and higher borrowing costs has left many low income countries with little opportunity to recover.

"I mean, we don't see really a light at the end of the tunnel," De Croo said. Generating jobs, especially at a time when increasing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete, is another top priority. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce in the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest a net creation of only 400 million new jobs. The UNDP announced this week a "Jobs for Prosperity" initiative that will work with governments, development banks such as the World Bank and private businesses to encourage investment in key job creating areas such as tourism, healthcare and food processing.

The initiative and other efforts will focus on helping countries attract investment by improving their governance and policies, while creating pipelines of "investible projects," De Croo said. "These are things that are feasible. It's been proven that you can do it in many places of the world.

item.title: Wholesale inflation jumps to 11.39% in September as food, fuel costs rise
item.description: India's wholesale inflation accelerated from 9.92 per cent in August as fuel and power prices climbed, food inflation quickened and factory-gate prices rose across several industries ...
item.dc:creator: Our Bureau
item.content:encoded: India's wholesale price inflation rose to 11.39 per cent in September from 9.92 per cent in August, driven by higher prices of fuel and power, food articles and manufactured products, according to provisional government data released on Wednesday. The Wholesale Price Index (WPI), with 2022-23 as its base year, increased to 112.5 in September from 110.8 in August. Wholesale inflation stood at 9.78 per cent in July, according to the final estimates released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The rise in wholesale inflation was broad-based, with all three major components of the index — primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products — recording higher year-on-year inflation in September.Fuel and power inflation rises to 25.85%Inflation in the fuel and power category accelerated to 25.85 per cent in September from 22.93 per cent in August, reflecting sustained price pressures across energy-related commodities. Within the category, inflation in crude petroleum and natural gas surged to 57.32 per cent from 34.41 per cent in August. Mineral oils, which include petroleum products, recorded inflation of 40.02 per cent, compared with 38.48 per cent in the previous month. Coal and lignite inflation also increased sharply to 9.31 per cent from 1.57 per cent. Electricity prices, however, continued to decline on a year-on-year basis, with inflation at minus 0.43 per cent in September, compared with minus 1.73 per cent in August.Wholesale food inflation climbs to 8.66%Food inflation also accelerated during September. The WPI Food Index, which combines food articles under primary articles and manufactured food products, recorded inflation of 8.66 per cent, compared with 7.05 per cent in August. Inflation in food articles increased to 8.14 per cent from 5.67 per cent in the previous month, contributing to the overall rise in wholesale prices. However, inflation in manufactured food products moderated marginally to 9.44 per cent in September from 9.65 per cent in August. Overall, inflation in primary articles rose to 8.67 per cent from 7.76 per cent in August. Within this category, inflation in non-food articles eased to 10.28 per cent from 14.79 per cent, while mineral inflation increased to 9.51 per cent from 8.24 per cent.Manufactured products inflation rises to 9.76%Inflation in manufactured products, which account for the largest share of the wholesale price index, increased to 9.76 per cent in September from 8.37 per cent in August. The increase was driven by higher prices across several industrial categories, including basic metals, chemicals, textiles, rubber and plastic products, and electrical equipment. Inflation in basic metals rose sharply to 16.96 per cent from 10.88 per cent in August, while inflation in chemicals and chemical products accelerated to 16.74 per cent from 14.30 per cent. Textile inflation increased to 13.85 per cent from 12.63 per cent, while rubber and plastic products recorded inflation of 13.47 per cent, compared with 11.18 per cent in August. Inflation in electrical equipment also increased to 11.93 per cent from 11.11 per cent. Meanwhile, inflation in computer, electronic and optical products turned positive at 4 per cent in September, compared with a contraction of 0.47 per cent in August.Cumulative WPI inflation at 9.85% in April-SeptemberAccording to the government data, cumulative wholesale inflation during April-September 2026 stood at 9.85 per cent, compared with a decline of 0.20 per cent during the corresponding period of the previous financial year. Fuel and power recorded cumulative inflation of 25.31 per cent during the first half of 2026-27, while inflation in manufactured products stood at 8.08 per cent. The cumulative WPI Food Index inflation was 6.10 per cent, compared with a contraction of 1.26 per cent during April-September 2025.Output and input producer price indices also increaseThe government also released provisional estimates of the Output Producer Price Index (PPI) and trial Input PPI for September. The all-India Output PPI for all commodities increased to 112.5 in September from 110.8 in August. Within the index, agriculture, forestry and fishing rose to 118.7 from 116.5, while mining and quarrying increased to 129.2 from 122.0. The index for manufactured products rose to 111.0 from 109.7. The trial Input PPI for the manufacturing sector increased to 106.1 in September from 104.2 in August, indicating a rise in the index of input costs faced by manufacturers. The government said the final WPI inflation rate for July remained unchanged at 9.78 per cent. The provisional WPI estimates for September were compiled with a weighted response rate of 83.4 per cent. The next WPI, Output PPI and trial Input PPI data, covering October 2026, will be released on November 16.
